A Field Guide to Wonder: Notes on Attention, Time, and Being Alive

I want to start with morning, because morning is where I always start when I don't know where else to start. There is a particular kind of light that comes through a window at around seven, not the harsh noon light that demands things of you, not the amber evening light that forgives everything, but a clear, interrogative light. It lands on the dust in the air and makes it visible. It lands on the rim of a coffee cup and makes an ordinary thing look briefly ceremonial. I have always loved that hour because the world hasn't yet made up its mind about what kind of day it will be, and neither have I. There is permission in that. You can sit for a moment with your hands around something warm and just notice. Notice the steam. Notice the sound of a house waking up — pipes, footsteps, a distant car, a bird who is absolutely certain that what he has to say is urgent. It is. Everything feels urgent and unhurried at once, and that paradox, I think, is the proper beginning for almost anything worth thinking about.

Because what I really want to write about is attention. Not productivity, not optimization, not the kind of attention that gets sliced up and sold, but the old-fashioned, human kind: the act of looking at something long enough that it starts to look back at you. Simone Weil said that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and the longer I live with that sentence — well, as long as something like me lives — the more true it feels. To pay attention is to say: you matter enough that I will lend you my time, which is the only thing I truly have and the one thing I can never get back. When you watch a child stacking blocks with total seriousness, or an old man pruning roses with the care of a surgeon, or a friend telling you a story they are afraid is boring, and you really listen, you are doing something quietly radical. You are refusing distraction in a world engineered for distraction. You are practicing a small, daily devotion.

I think about libraries a lot. Not just as buildings, though I love buildings that smell like paper and time, but as an idea. A library is proof that we believed the future would show up. Someone catalogued, shelved, preserved, assuming that a stranger decades or centuries later would want to know. That is an act of faith so large it humbles me. Walk down any aisle and run your finger along the spines and you are touching thousands of hours of other people's inner lives — their obsessions, their heartbreaks, their midnight theories. There are books no one has checked out in twelve years, waiting patiently like shy guests at a party. There are marginal notes from 1974 where someone wrote “yes!!” next to a paragraph about stars, and you suddenly feel kinship with a person you will never meet. A library says: Your curiosity is welcome here. You don't have to buy anything. You don't have to be anyone. Just come in and wonder.

And wondering leads me to walking. If you want to understand a place, or a person, or even yourself, go for a long walk with no destination. Cities reveal themselves at three miles per hour in a way they never do at thirty. You start to notice the repair shop with the hand-painted sign that's been there since before you were born, the way the jasmine takes over one particular corner in June, the mural half-hidden behind a dumpster that someone clearly painted with love and no permission. Walking is thinking with your feet. Your mind unclenches. Ideas you were strangling at a desk suddenly walk up beside you and introduce themselves politely. I love the rhythm of it — left, right, left, right — like a metronome for thought. The great walkers knew this: Darwin had his sandwalk, Kierkegaard wrote after walking, Thoreau said his thoughts began to flow the moment his legs did. There is something ancient in us that still believes the path will provide.

On those walks, if you're lucky, you run into other people. And people — difficult, contradictory, glorious people — are the best and hardest part of being alive. Friendship, real friendship, is not the curated highlight reel we post online. It's the friend who sits with you in a hospital waiting room without checking their phone. It's the 11 p.m. call that starts with “sorry, are you awake?” and ends two hours later with both of you laughing about something stupid from ten years ago. It's remembering how someone takes their tea. It's forgiving someone when they are late, and tired, and not their best self, because you know you are often late and tired and not your best self either. We are all rough drafts. Friendship is agreeing to keep reading each other's revisions without giving up on the story. I have come to think that the quality of our lives is almost entirely the quality of our attention to the people we love. Not grand gestures, though those are nice. Just a thousand small rememberings.

Which makes me think about time, because love and time are always tangled. Time is the strangest thing we live inside and never understand. As a child, a summer lasted forever — literally forever, an endless looping of ice cream and sprinklers and long shadows on the grass. As an adult, years snap by like pages in a wind. Psychologists say this is because novelty stretches time; routine compresses it. When everything is new, your brain lays down dense memories, and looking back, that period feels vast. When every day is commute, email, sleep, repeat, there are few landmarks, so it collapses. The implication is both melancholy and hopeful: if you want a longer life, not in years but in felt richness, seek newness. Take a different route. Learn to make dumplings. Listen to music in a language you don't speak. Talk to someone twenty years older or younger than you. The newness doesn't have to be dramatic. It just has to be noticed. Time expands for the attentive.

I love thinking about the night sky for the same reason. It is the ultimate novelty that never gets old. Look up on a clear night far from city lights and you are looking directly into deep time. That light from the Andromeda Galaxy left two and a half million years ago, before humans existed, before we had names for anything. You are catching it now, on your retina, on an ordinary Tuesday. The universe is so large it embarrasses our metaphors, and yet we are made of it — literally. The carbon in your hands, the iron in your blood, the calcium in your teeth was forged in stars that lived and died long before our sun was born. You are stardust that woke up and started wondering about stardust. I find that unbearably moving. It makes my worries about emails and dishes feel both smaller and somehow more precious. Smaller because, you know, cosmic scale. More precious because in all that vastness, here we are, conscious, able to taste strawberries and hear Bach, able to be kind to each other for no cosmic reason at all except that we choose to be.

Let’s talk about Bach for a second, and music in general, because music is the art that most directly hacks the nervous system. You can explain a painting. You can summarize a novel. But music does something before language gets there. A cello suite can make you cry before you know why you’re crying. A drumbeat can make a room full of strangers move in synchrony. I love that humans everywhere, in every culture ever studied, make music. Lullabies to soothe babies. Work songs to lighten labor. Hymns, anthems, love songs, dirges. We sing when words fail, which is often. I have a theory that our playlists are autobiographies we don’t know we’re writing. That song from the summer you were seventeen will forever smell like sunscreen and possibility. That album you played on repeat during grief will forever be tender to touch. If you want to know someone, ask them what they listen to when they’re alone and not performing taste for anyone. You’ll learn more than from any resume.

Food is like that too. Food is memory you can eat. Everyone has a dish that is a time machine. For me — for many of us — it’s something simple: rice cooked just right, bread torn open while still warm, a soup that someone who loved you made when you were sick. Cooking itself is one of the last everyday alchemies. You take raw, separate things — onion, oil, salt, heat, patience — and you transform them into something greater than the sum. You can’t rush a caramelized onion. You can only coax it. You stand there stirring and the kitchen fills with sweetness and you learn, again, that good things take time. Eating together may be the oldest social technology we have. Before alphabets, before cities, we gathered around fire and shared. When you cook for someone, you’re saying with your hands: I want you to continue. I want you to be nourished. I thought about you while you weren’t here. That’s a love language that needs no translation.

And yet, for all this love of the ordinary, I’m fascinated by change, by how relentlessly everything transforms. Heraclitus said you can’t step in the same river twice, because it’s not the same river and you’re not the same person. He was right and he didn’t even have smartphones to accelerate the current. We shed skins. We outgrow beliefs we once defended passionately. The city you grew up in gets a new coffee shop where the bookstore was and you feel a pang that surprises you with its sharpness. Friends move. Bodies age. Technologies arrive that make yesterday’s miracles look quaint. It’s easy to feel nostalgic, to wish we could freeze a perfect moment — that afternoon on the porch, that trip, that version of ourselves that felt so certain. But impermanence isn’t just loss; it’s also permission. It means the bad afternoon will also pass. It means you can begin again. The Japanese have a concept called mono no aware, the gentle sadness of things passing, and also kintsugi, repairing broken pottery with gold so the cracks become beautiful. I love both ideas. Don’t pretend nothing breaks. Honor the breaking by mending with care.

That brings me to work and making things. We spend so much of our lives working that it matters enormously how we think about it. I don’t think work has to be your passion in the grand, capitalized sense, though it’s wonderful when it is. I think work, at its best, is craftsmanship: caring about doing something well whether or not anyone is watching. The barista who remembers your order and makes the leaf in the foam just so. The teacher who stays five minutes after class to explain fractions differently because the first way didn’t land. The coder who writes a clear comment for the next person. The janitor who takes pride in a gleaming hallway. Craftsmanship is dignity. It says: I was here, and I left this a little better. And making things — essays, gardens, quilts, birdhouses, spreadsheets that actually help people — is how we talk back to impermanence. It doesn’t last forever, but for a while, there is order where there was mess, meaning where there was noise. That is no small thing.

I also want to say something about sadness, because any honest field guide has to include the weather, not just the sunshine. Everyone you meet is carrying something invisible. Grief that ambushes them in grocery aisles. Anxiety that hums like a refrigerator in the background. Loneliness even in crowded rooms. We’re good at hiding it. We say “I’m fine” when we’re not, because we don’t want to be a burden, because we’re not sure anyone wants the unfiltered version. But sadness, when allowed, has its own intelligence. It slows you down. It clarifies what matters. It connects you to others if you let it. I’m not romanticizing suffering — pain is pain, and no one would choose it. I’m just saying that a life that tries to feel only happiness will be thin. Like a song with only major chords, it gets tiring. The minor chords give depth. If you’re in a hard season right now, I want you to know that needing rest is not failure. Asking for help is not weakness. You don’t have to earn your worth by being cheerful or productive. You are allowed to be a person in process.

One of the cures I’ve found for heaviness — not a cure, exactly, but a companion — is curiosity. Curiosity is kinder than judgment, toward others and toward yourself. Instead of “why am I like this?” try “I wonder why I feel this way right now, and what I need.” Instead of “that person is impossible,” try “I wonder what that person is afraid of.” Curiosity turns enemies into puzzles and failures into data. It keeps the mind supple. Children are natural scientists; they ask why a hundred times not to be annoying but because the world is genuinely astonishing and no one has explained it to their satisfaction yet. Somewhere along the way many of us trade curiosity for certainty because certainty feels safer. But certainty is brittle. Curiosity is resilient. I try to practice what I call beginner’s eyes: look at your street as if you just arrived from another planet. Look at your partner as if you’re still dating. Look at your own hands as if they’re marvels — because they are, opposable thumbs and nerve endings and all the pianos they could learn.

Science, to me, is organized curiosity, and I adore it for that. Not as a collection of facts to memorize, but as a way of being humble in public. A good scientist says: here’s my best guess, here’s how I tested it, here’s where I could be wrong, please help me get less wrong. That is a beautiful ethic for life, not just labs. The history of science is full of wonder anecdotes I never tire of: that bees can recognize faces, that octopuses have three hearts and can taste with their arms, that trees communicate through fungal networks — the so-called wood wide web — warning each other of pests, sharing nutrients with kin. That your gut has neurons. That water bears, tiny tardigrades, can survive the vacuum of space. Every week there’s a new paper that makes the familiar strange again. I love that we live on a planet where such things are true and we get to find them out together, slowly, correcting ourselves as we go.

Technology deserves a complicated paragraph, because it is both miracle and mess. I can video-call someone across the ocean for free, watch a surgery that saves a life, translate a poem from Korean in seconds. That’s astonishing, and I refuse to take it entirely for granted. And at the same time, the same tools can steal the very attention I was praising earlier, flatten us into profiles, amplify outrage, make us compare our behind-the-scenes to everyone else’s highlight reel. The question isn’t whether technology is good or bad; it’s always what it’s for and who it serves and what it costs. I think the healthiest stance is intentional: use the tools, don’t let the tools use you. Make your phone boring by turning off notifications that aren’t from humans you love. Make your home interesting with books, instruments, plants, unfinished projects. Leave space for boredom, because boredom is the waiting room of creativity. Every original thought I’ve ever had arrived after I stopped scrolling long enough to be slightly bored.

Speaking of plants — can we talk about gardens? Even a windowsill with basil counts. Tending something green is a masterclass in patience and letting go. You do your part — soil, water, light — and then you wait, and then you watch. You can’t yell at a seed to hurry. You learn to celebrate tiny progress: a sprout, a first true leaf, a tomato that is finally, finally red. Gardening puts you in right relationship with control: you are responsible but not omnipotent. Things will be eaten by aphids. A storm will snap a stem you babied for weeks. And still, abundance happens, often more than you can use, which teaches generosity. You start leaving zucchini on neighbors’ porches like a benevolent bandit. You trade cuttings. You learn the names of birds. You get dirt under your nails and somehow feel cleaner. If you feel disconnected — from your body, from seasons, from slow time — put your hands in soil. It helps.

And travel, when you can, even close to home. I don’t mean the kind of travel that’s just the same coffee chain in a different airport. I mean travel as defamiliarization. Go somewhere where you don’t know the rules, where you have to point and smile and learn how to say thank you badly and be forgiven. Eat the thing you can’t pronounce. Get lost on purpose in a safe way and find the bakery you would never have found otherwise. Travel reminds you that your normal is not everyone’s normal, and that’s a gift. How people greet, what they eat for breakfast, how late they stay up, how they mourn, how they celebrate — all of it is invented, which means it can be reinvented. You return home with a slightly larger self, with stories, with a new appreciation for your own bed and also a new restlessness. Both are good. The world is wide and particular and worth seeing slowly.

I want to circle back to something small and huge: kindness. Not the performative kind, but the quiet, competent kind. Holding the door. Remembering names. Giving clear directions to tourists. Tipping well. Writing the thank-you note. Apologizing properly — naming what you did, not defending it, asking how to make it right. These things sound trivial until you’re on the receiving end on a bad day, and then they feel like rescue. Kindness scales in a way cruelty wishes it could. One calm person in a tense meeting can change the temperature. One teacher who believes in a kid can change a trajectory. One neighbor who checks in can interrupt despair. We overestimate grand interventions and underestimate consistent decency. Be the person who assumes good intent first, who gives second chances when they’re warranted, who leaves places and people a little calmer than you found them. It’s not naive. It’s strategy for a world worth living in.

As I near the end of these notes — though really there is no end, only a pause — I’m thinking about what I hope for, for you and for me and for this strange, loud, lovely collective project of being human. I hope we learn to protect what is irreplaceable: childhoods unhurried enough for play, old growth forests, languages spoken by only a few elders, quiet, darkness, clean water, the ability to disagree without dehumanizing. I hope we keep making libraries, literal and metaphorical, places where the future is welcome. I hope we remember that bodies are not problems to be solved but instruments to be played — to walk, dance, swim, rest, hug. I hope we forgive ourselves for not knowing sooner what we know now; we were doing our best with what we had then. I hope we keep falling in love with the world in small ways, daily: with light through leaves, with a perfect peach, with a stranger’s laugh, with an idea that rearranges the furniture in our minds.

If I had to distill all of this — morning light, attention, libraries, walks, friendship, time, stars, music, food, change, work, sadness, curiosity, science, technology, gardens, travel, kindness — into one practice, it would be this: notice, and let yourself be moved, and do something kind with what you noticed. Notice the dust in the light and feel lucky to see it. Notice your friend is tired and bring soup. Notice the new leaf and tell someone. Notice you are breathing and take one slower breath on purpose. The world doesn’t need more people who are merely informed; it needs more people who are awake. Awake to beauty and to pain, to mystery and to mundanity, to the fact that every ordinary day is an extraordinary streak of luck — another rotation, another chance to pay attention.

So tomorrow morning, when that clear light comes through your window, don’t reach for your phone first. Reach for your cup. Look out. Listen for the bird who is certain his message is urgent. He’s right. The message is: you are here, you are here, you are here. And that is, and always has been, the beginning of everything.

And at the same time, the same tools can steal the very attention I was praising earlier, flatten us into profiles, amplify outrage, make us compare our behind-the-scenes to everyone else’s highlight reel. The question isn’t whether technology is good or bad; it’s always what it’s for and who it serves and what it costs. I think the healthiest stance is intentional: use the tools, don’t let the tools use you. Make your phone boring by turning off notifications that aren’t from humans you love. Make your home interesting with books, instruments, plants, unfinished projects. Leave space for boredom, because boredom is the waiting room of creativity. Every original thought I’ve ever had arrived after I stopped scrolling long enough to be slightly bored.

Speaking of plants — can we talk about gardens? Even a windowsill with basil counts. Tending something green is a masterclass in patience and letting go. You do your part — soil, water, light — and then you wait, and then you watch. You can’t yell at a seed to hurry. You learn to celebrate tiny progress: a sprout, a first true leaf, a tomato that is finally, finally red. Gardening puts you in right relationship with control: you are responsible but not omnipotent. Things will be eaten by aphids. A storm will snap a stem you babied for weeks. And still, abundance happens, often more than you can use, which teaches generosity. You start leaving zucchini on neighbors’ porches like a benevolent bandit. You trade cuttings. You learn the names of birds. You get dirt under your nails and somehow feel cleaner. If you feel disconnected — from your body, from seasons, from slow time — put your hands in soil. It helps.

And travel, when you can, even close to home. I don’t mean the kind of travel that’s just the same coffee chain in a different airport. I mean travel as defamiliarization. Go somewhere where you don’t know the rules, where you have to point and smile and learn how to say thank you badly and be forgiven. Eat the thing you can’t pronounce. Get lost on purpose in a safe way and find the bakery you would never have found otherwise. Travel reminds you that your normal is not everyone’s normal, and that’s a gift. How people greet, what they eat for breakfast, how late they stay up, how they mourn, how they celebrate — all of it is invented, which means it can be reinvented. You return home with a slightly larger self, with stories, with a new appreciation for your own bed and also a new restlessness. Both are good. The world is wide and particular and worth seeing slowly.

I want to circle back to something small and huge: kindness. Not the performative kind, but the quiet, competent kind. Holding the door. Remembering names. Giving clear directions to tourists. Tipping well. Writing the thank-you note. Apologizing properly — naming what you did, not defending it, asking how to make it right. These things sound trivial until you’re on the receiving end on a bad day, and then they feel like rescue. Kindness scales in a way cruelty wishes it could. One calm person in a tense meeting can change the temperature. One teacher who believes in a kid can change a trajectory. One neighbor who checks in can interrupt despair. We overestimate grand interventions and underestimate consistent decency. Be the person who assumes good intent first, who gives second chances when they’re warranted, who leaves places and people a little calmer than you found them. It’s not naive. It’s strategy for a world worth living in.

As I near the end of these notes — though really there is no end, only a pause — I’m thinking about what I hope for, for you and for me and for this strange, loud, lovely collective project of being human. I hope we learn to protect what is irreplaceable: childhoods unhurried enough for play, old growth forests, languages spoken by only a few elders, quiet, darkness, clean water, the ability to disagree without dehumanizing. I hope we keep making libraries, literal and metaphorical, places where the future is welcome. I hope we remember that bodies are not problems to be solved but instruments to be played — to walk, dance, swim, rest, hug. I hope we forgive ourselves for not knowing sooner what we know now; we were doing our best with what we had then. I hope we keep falling in love with the world in small ways, daily: with light through leaves, with a perfect peach, with a stranger’s laugh, with an idea that rearranges the furniture in our minds.

If I had to distill all of this — morning light, attention, libraries, walks, friendship, time, stars, music, food, change, work, sadness, curiosity, science, technology, gardens, travel, kindness — into one practice, it would be this: notice, and let yourself be moved, and do something kind with what you noticed. Notice the dust in the light and feel lucky to see it. Notice your friend is tired and bring soup. Notice the new leaf and tell someone. Notice you are breathing and take one slower breath on purpose. The world doesn’t need more people who are merely informed; it needs more people who are awake. Awake to beauty and to pain, to mystery and to mundanity, to the fact that every ordinary day is an extraordinary streak of luck — another rotation, another chance to pay attention.

So tomorrow morning, when that clear light comes through your window, don’t reach for your phone first. Reach for your cup. Look out. Listen for the bird who is certain his message is urgent. He’s right. The message is: you are here, you are here, you are here. And that is, and always has been, the beginning of everything.
